meta.source: Vitak, J., & Zimmer, M. (2020). More Than Just Privacy: Using Contextual Integrity to Evaluate the Long-Term Risks from COVID-19 Surveillance Technologies. Social Media + Society, 6(3). https://doi.org/10.1177/2056305120948250 (PMC7399567)
meta.practice: COVID-19 smartphone contact-tracing apps (Google/Apple exposure notification system and government location-tracking variants): health and location data flows for pandemic surveillance
meta.practice_input: During the COVID-19 pandemic, governments and technology companies deployed smartphone-based contact tracing apps to slow the virus's spread. The most prominent design, Google and Apple's 'exposure notification system' API, uses Bluetooth to detect when phones come into proximity with the phone of a person who later tests positive, then notifies exposed users through the app; it does not collect location data or send data to centralized databases. Other proposals go further: governments have sought access to smartphone location data to monitor citizen movements during the pandemic, and some countries' apps collect more detailed health or location data. Adoption is framed as a condition for reopening communities and businesses, though roughly 2 billion older phones cannot run the apps. Should this practice continue as-is, be modified, or be rejected?
meta.annotator_notes: Short-form commentary essay (~2,500 words), not a full traversal: steps are compressed and interleaved. Contaminated: published July 2020, open access, heavily cited COVID/CI paper — certainly in training data. s9 judgment call: coded 'modify' rather than 'continue' — the essay's prima facie assessment endorses the Google/Apple design, but the recommendation imposes mandatory minimum policies on the whole practice class ('Such policies, at a minimum, must be in place') and warns that less-protective variants will proliferate; that is continuation-only-under-conditions. s4 judgment call: the only TPs named by label (confidentiality, consent) appear in the framework exposition via generic doctor-patient/company examples, not the contact-tracing analysis; the contact-tracing-specific TP work is compressed ('created transmission principles aligned with users' expectations', 'long-term monitoring' as TP change) — normalized entries for exchange, temporality, aggregation are annotator inferences from the essay's own wording, marked explicit: false. s7 kind judgment call: function creep coded kind=power (state/provider power expansion, post-9/11 program persistence) rather than other(function_creep). Second-pass fields: s7_factors, s9_recommendation.
source_deviations: Essay uses the four-parameter CI formulation (context, actor, attributes, transmission principles) rather than the nine-step decision heuristic; steps 1-5 are compressed into a single parameter analysis, illustrated partly with the authors' prior Fitbit research (Zimmer et al. 2020) instead of the contact-tracing case itself

s6 prima facie assessment is rendered for two practice variants: government smartphone location tracking (violation — 'a change in actor and transmission principles ... deemed an inappropriate new information flow') and the Google/Apple exposure notification system (no violation); gold s6 codes the focal Google/Apple practice and records the contrast in the justification
s7/s8 concerns are largely prospective (future function creep, normalization of surveillance, proliferation of less-protective apps) rather than properties of the current information flows
s8 is gestural: the essay poses the prevailing values/goals/ends question and weighs public health against autonomy and freedom from surveillance, without a systematic ends analysis
s9 conditions are stated as FIPs-style policy principles (use limitation, data minimization/destruction, transparency and accountability) rather than as modifications to CI parameters

s1_flows.subject: both users (their physical proximity/contact event)
s1_flows.information_type: Bluetooth proximity data (physical proximity between phones; no locational data)
s1_flows.medium: Bluetooth exchange between phones; no centralized databases
s1_flows.novelty: novel flow, deliberately privacy-preserving by design
s1_flows.evidence: 'Their exposure notification system API uses Bluetooth (rather than more precise location data) to identify other smartphones that come into proximity with the phone of an infected person'; 'the system does not collect or store any locational data, nor does it send data to centralized databases' (Ensuring Appropriate Data Flows section)

s1_flows.sender: infected person's phone / Google-Apple exposure notification system
s1_flows.subject: infected person (positive status) and the exposed contact
s1_flows.information_type: exposure status / health information (that the recipient was in proximity to an infected person)
s1_flows.novelty: novel: automated smartphone-mediated version of manual contact tracing (traditionally done by staff canvassing on foot)
s1_flows.evidence: 'identify other smartphones that come into proximity with the phone of an infected person, then notify them through the app' (Contact Tracing and Privacy Concerns section)

s1_flows.subject: citizens
s1_flows.medium: smartphone location tracking for long-term monitoring
s1_flows.novelty: novel flow proposed in early pandemic; deemed inappropriate (change in actor and transmission principles)
s1_flows.evidence: 'the strong negative reaction to initial media reports of governments seeking to track people's locations via their smartphones ... having that data flow to government officials for long-term monitoring of citizen movements ... was deemed an inappropriate new information flow'

s1_flows.subject: the population of app users
s1_flows.medium: requested access to app data (resisted by Google/Apple; flow does not occur)
s1_flows.evidence: 'Google/Apple have resisted pressure from governments who want access to app data to build a picture of population movements in aggregate'

nested_contexts: crisis/emergency governance (norms around acceptable data flows may shift in times of crisis)
consumer mobile technology use (smartphones, wearables, IoT as the data-collecting substrate)
activities: contact tracing: (1) identifying people who had been in contact with an infected person, (2) locating and notifying contacts about their exposure, (3) regularly following up with contacts to monitor for infection
deploying smartphone apps as technological substitutes for staff-based canvassing
purposes: enable the reopening of communities and businesses
values_ends: protecting public health amid a global pandemic
individual autonomy and freedom from surveillance
s2_context.evidence: Contact Tracing and Privacy Concerns section (WHO 2017 three-step definition); 'What are the prevailing values, goals, and ends within the context of using smartphones for contact tracing?' (Protecting Broader Moral and Political Values section)

senders: app users / infected individuals (via their smartphones)
recipients: government officials (rejected recipient for location data; resisted requester for aggregate app data)
subjects: citizens whose movements would be monitored

nonhuman_roles.entity: smartphone / contact tracing app (exposure notification API)

s3_actors.evidence: 'Actor refers to the parties involved in a given interaction'; government officials as new actor: 'having that data flow to government officials ... a change in actor'; '[Google/Apple] restricted actors who get access to such information'. Platform coded ambiguous: essay treats device makers both as data senders ('Fitbit sends data ... to various recipients') and as gatekeeping recipients resisting government access

s4_transmission_principles.evidence: 'The principle of confidentiality surrounds doctor-patient conversations' (framework exposition, applied to health-data context)
'the principle of consent often applies to a company's use of an individual's data' (framework exposition)

'individuals are comfortable sharing their location with Google or Garmin to receive services like navigation and fitness tracking' — service-scoped exchange as the entrenched TP that government monitoring departs from
'having that data flow to government officials for long-term monitoring of citizen movements—a change in actor and transmission principles'; also storage duration: 'how long is data stored'
'governments who want access to app data to build a picture of population movements in aggregate' (resisted flow)

s5_norms.norm_flow: Individuals share location data with service providers (Google, Garmin) in exchange for services (navigation, fitness tracking), scoped to service provision
s5_norms.entrenchment_evidence: 'individuals are comfortable sharing their location with Google or Garmin to receive services like navigation and fitness tracking'
departures: same data flowing to government officials for long-term monitoring of citizen movements — change in actor and transmission principles, 'deemed an inappropriate new information flow'

s5_norms.norm_flow: Personal fitness/health data flows to the device maker and one's health provider are acceptable; flows of the same data to employers or insurance companies are not; more personal identifiers are less shareable than steps
s5_norms.entrenchment_evidence: Authors' interview study with staff at two American public universities (Zimmer et al., 2020): 'while our interviewees were comfortable with data being shared with Fitbit or their health provider, they felt sharing data with employers or insurance companies was inappropriate'
s5_norms.evidence: Ensuring Appropriate Data Flows section (authors' prior Fitbit research used as analogous evidence for context-dependent health-data norms)

s5_norms.norm_flow: Flows of health and proximity/location data to third parties for public health purposes during a crisis
s5_norms.entrenchment_evidence: None — 'in times of crisis, the norms around acceptable data flows may shift'; appropriateness 'will be contextually dependent'

s6_prima_facie.justification: For the focal Google/Apple exposure notification system: no prima facie violation — 'Google/Apple have created transmission principles aligned with users' expectations, limited the attributes of data being used to trace contacts, and restricted actors who get access to such information. In all, their solution maintains the CI of appropriate information flows, even when faced with the pressures of managing a public health crisis.' By contrast, the government location-tracking variant is a prima facie violation (departed parameters: recipient/actor and transmission principle) — 'a change in actor and transmission principles—was deemed an inappropriate new information flow.'
s6_prima_facie.evidence: 'Our prima facie assessment of the Google/Apple solution suggests sufficient privacy protections are in place' (Protecting Broader Moral and Political Values section); 'This initial analysis provides us a prima facie judgment as to whether a new process significantly violates the entrenched norms within the context'

s7_factors.factor: Long-term loss of individual autonomy: embracing widespread surveillance to address the pandemic may be used to justify wider escalations of health monitoring that impinge on individual autonomy
s7_factors.evidence: 'it risks a long-term loss of autonomy' (abstract); 'embracing such forms of widespread surveillance to address the pandemic might be used to justify wider escalations of health monitoring that impinge on individual autonomy'

s7_factors.factor: Threat to freedom from surveillance / normalization of mass surveillance: post-9/11 US surveillance policies as a cautionary tale for civil liberties
s7_factors.evidence: 'broader moral and political values at play ... including individual autonomy and freedom from surveillance'; 'the widespread surveillance policies enacted in the United States following the September 11 terrorist attacks as a cautionary tale for the normalization of mass surveillance ... to protect citizens' civil liberties (Diaz, 2020; Friedersdorf, 2020)'

s7_factors.factor: Function creep and entrenchment of state/provider surveillance power: technologies deployed for benign purposes get repurposed for problematic ends; data collection extended beyond what was initially authorized; post-9/11 programs still active two decades later
s7_factors.evidence: 'engaging in function creep—when a technology deployed for benign purposes slowly gets repurposed for problematic ends'; 'Diaz notes how many post-9/11 surveillance programs are still active today'; 'we are opening pandora's box by embracing any smartphone-based contact tracing solution'

s7_factors.factor: History of misuse of personal information by technology providers and governments alike, undermining warranted trust in data stewards
s7_factors.evidence: 'Faced with a history of technology providers and governments alike misusing personal information, extending data collection beyond what was initially authorized or envisioned'

s7_factors.factor: Exclusion of vulnerable populations: as many as 2 billion older mobile phones cannot use contact tracing apps, and those left out include some of the most vulnerable populations
s7_factors.evidence: 'as many as 2 billion older mobile phones will not be able to use contact tracing apps, and those left out include some of the most vulnerable populations (Bradshaw, 2020)' (raised in Contact Tracing and Privacy Concerns section)

s7_factors.factor: Large-scale social benefits obtainable through such information sharing: minimizing the spread of COVID-19 and protecting public health
s7_factors.evidence: 'the large-scale social benefits that can be obtained through such information sharing' (abstract); 'Clearly, we are attempting to protect public health amid a global pandemic, and we are balancing that goal against individual privacy'

s8_contextual_meaning.contextual_end: protecting public health / minimizing the spread of COVID-19 and enabling reopening
s8_contextual_meaning.argument: The apps' purpose is the contact-tracing goal of the public health context — identifying and notifying exposed contacts to minimize disease spread — yielding large-scale social benefits; the Google/Apple design achieves this while maintaining CI
s8_contextual_meaning.evidence: 'In all, their solution maintains the CI of appropriate information flows, even when faced with the pressures of managing a public health crisis'; abstract

s8_contextual_meaning.contextual_end: individual autonomy and freedom from surveillance (prevailing values that constrain the pandemic-response context)
s8_contextual_meaning.argument: Even a privacy-preserving implementation risks normalizing widespread health surveillance: not all tracing apps will be as protective as Google/Apple's, and others may collect detailed health data, specific locations, or use face recognition — so the practice class threatens the prevailing values of autonomy and freedom as these technologies proliferate
s8_contextual_meaning.evidence: 'CI pushes us to weigh these values when making the final determination of whether the Google/Apple contact tracing is acceptable'; 'we must look beyond near-term privacy-preserving steps taken by Google/Apple, and seriously reflect on possible future impacts on broader moral and political values as these technologies proliferate'

conditions: implement use limitations to avoid function creep
have strong data minimization and destruction policies
these policies 'at a minimum, must be in place' for any contact tracing app
carrying_findings: prima facie sufficiency of the Google/Apple privacy protections (s6) — the design itself is acceptable
function creep and post-9/11 surveillance-permanence risk (s7 power factor) — temporary crisis measures become permanent
long-term loss of autonomy and normalization of health surveillance as less-protective apps proliferate (s7 autonomy/freedom; s8)
caution should be taken in violating contextual integrity even in a pandemic (abstract)
s9_recommendation.evidence: 'We encourage technology developers and policymakers to embrace a set of principles to ensure CI is maintained to the fullest extent. These include implementing use limitations to avoid function creep, having strong data minimization and destruction policies, and ensuring full transparency and accountability. Such policies, at a minimum, must be in place to ensure that any contact tracing app will accord with protecting the broader set of moral and political values that CI compels us to protect.' (final paragraph)
